newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Slowing economy hits S.Korea's Feb vehicle sales.
newsitem.headline: Slowing economy hits S.Korea's Feb vehicle sales.

text.p: South Korea's vehicle sales dropped 4.7 percent in February after being battered by a slowing economy, rising petrol prices and a weak yen, the Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association said on Wednesday.
The association said 185,610 vehicles were sold in February, down from 194,800 units a year earlier.
"The slowing economy dampened domestic sales, while the yen's fall against the dollar hit exports," said an association official.
A weaker yen tends to make Japanese exports less expensive and, thus, more attractive.
Consumers were also cutting back spending on durable goods, including cars, expecting a further economic slowdown.
Domestic vehicle sales in February totalled 105,990 units, down 3.9 percent from 110,236 units a year before. Exports fell 5.8 percent to 79,620 units from 84,564, the association said.
"A surge in petrol prices also chilled domestic demand," said the official.
Petrol prices are hovering at between 835 ($0.97) and 846 won per litre, sharply higher than about 610 won a year ago, according to the Trade Ministry.
Analysts said sales were also hit by consumers postponing purchases to wait for new models.
Hyundai Motor Co's new minivan, Starex, began to roll out from March and the sub-compact MX car, which will compete with Daewoo Motor Co's Tico, will hit the road in the second half of 1997.
Kia Motors Corp will begin marketing luxury Enterprise sedans in March and an upgrade of its compact sedan Sephia in June.
Daewoo, a unit of the Daewoo Group, started selling Nubira compact cars from February and plans to introduce a larger Leganza sedan in April.

The nation's largest car maker, Hyundai, said its vehicle sales in February fell to 82,471 units from 87,244 a year earlier. It said domestic sales dropped to 46,471 units from 49,629, and exports fell to 36,000 units from 37,215.
"Sales in February was also slow because of the aftermath of labour unrest in January," Hyundai spokesman Min Kyong-hwan said.
Nationwide wildcat strikes began late in December to protest the forced passage of a labour law that lets companies lay off workers and replace strikers. Parliament is reviewing the law.

Hyundai Motor, flagship unit of the Hyundai Group, reported its vehicle sales for January plunged to 48,432 units from 106,885 a year ago. The manufacturers' association said exports were undermined by Daewoo Motor's plans to sell inventories before introducing new models to overseas customers.
"Daewoo will soon agressively export new models like Nubira. But until then, its overseas sales will be very low," said the association official.
Daewoo exported only 7,959 vehicles in February, sharply down from 25,832 a year ago, the association said. Its domestic sales rose to 15,605 units in the month, compared with 9,266.
Kia Motors reported its domestic sales fell to 27,407 units in February from 32,315 a year ago, while exports, including shipments of knock-down kits, rose to 29,015 units from 22,012.
